media_strategy.selection_principle: default to all five channels (chart, image, video, audio, interactive_or_map); each chosen from the data's properties — a fixed 1,440-minute budget, 25 flagged countries, and six decades of trend.

chart.reason: The dataset is a set of weighted minute-per-day comparisons, rankings and decade trends — inherently chart-shaped.

image.reason: A single atmospheric 24-hour-clock hero sets the 'a day in a life' frame that pure numbers cannot.

video.reason: Animating the hero into a day-to-night time-lapse embodies the 1,440-minute cycle that the whole piece is built on.

audio.reason: The screen-time decade trend is a short rising ranked sequence — sonified and synced to its line chart so the reader hears the climb. Visual fallback always present.

interactive_or_map.reason: 25 flagged countries invite an explorable sortable ranking; the central finding invites a guess-first reveal of the gendered day.

media_blockers.reason: image2video (veo-3.1-fast) ultimately unavailable. Attempt 1 rejected aspect-ratio 1:1 (HTTP 400 INVALID_ARGUMENT); attempts 2 and 3 at 16:9 failed with 'service experiencing high load' (provider-side). Teaser falls back to the still hero image (des_02) animated with a CSS Ken-Burns / gradient drift so the day-to-night feel is preserved without the generated clip.

des_01.label: Teaser — 24-hour clock hero (video unavailable; CSS-animated still fallback)

content.fallback_from: image2video (veo-3.1-fast) failed on provider high-load; see meta.media_blockers
content.animation: CSS slow Ken-Burns zoom + a soft warm-to-cool gradient overlay that drifts dawn->night, ~18s loop, prefers-reduced-motion respected

des_01.brief: Full-viewport hero of the 24-hour clock with silhouettes of daily life around the dial. Because the generated time-lapse clip failed (provider load), the teaser is the still hero.png with a gentle CSS Ken-Burns zoom and a drifting day-to-night gradient overlay so the cyclical feeling survives. No headline text baked in.
des_01.rationale: The whole piece is about how one fixed day is divided; opening on the clock makes the reader feel the 1,440-minute frame before a single number. CSS motion preserves the day-night intent without the generated video.

des_02.label: Hero still (poster / fallback)

content.prompt: Cinematic 24-hour clock dissolving into a dawn-to-night gradient sky with silhouettes of everyday domestic life arranged around the dial, painterly, teal and amber, no text

des_02.brief: The still version of the teaser, reused inside the hook section as an atmospheric anchor beside the lead finding, and as the video poster.
des_02.rationale: Reusing the hero still keeps the visual language cohesive and guarantees a graceful fallback for the teaser video.

des_03.label: Lead chart — the gendered work day

content.interaction: hover tooltip with exact minutes and h:mm

des_03.brief: Four paired horizontal bars (Paid work, Housework, Childcare, Total work), men vs women. Women's Housework bar dwarfs men's; the Total work pair is highlighted to show women's bar extends 32.5 min further despite men's longer paid bar. Convert minutes to h:mm in tooltips.
des_03.rationale: A grouped bar makes the asymmetry instantly legible: men lead on paid, women lead far more on unpaid, and the total flips against men.

des_04.label: Guess-first — the gendered day

content.initial_state: Prompt: 'Women do X times as much unpaid work as men. Drag to guess X.' A slider from 1.0x to 4.0x with a live readout.
content.trigger: Reader drags the slider and clicks 'Reveal'
content.transition: The true value 2.26x snaps into place; the reader's guess and the truth are shown side by side
content.payoff: Reveal text: women average 236.8 min of unpaid work to men's 104.9 — 2.26x — then the lead chart (des_03) scrolls into view

des_04.brief: A single-slider guess-first widget that asks readers to commit to the unpaid-work ratio before seeing it. Cheap to build, vanilla JS, maximises the surprise of the 2.26x figure. Pairs with the lead chart below.
des_04.rationale: The lead finding is counterintuitive enough that letting readers guess first lands harder than presenting the number cold.

des_05.label: The average day — stacked 1,440-minute bar

content.interaction: hover each segment for activity + minutes + h:mm + share of day

des_05.brief: One long horizontal bar representing a full 1,440-minute day, segmented by activity (Sleep largest, then screen, paid work, housework, etc.). Axis labelled to 1,440. Reinforces that every activity competes for the same fixed budget.
des_05.rationale: A single stacked day-bar visually argues the core constraint of time-use research: the day is zero-sum.

des_06.label: Sleep ranking with national flags (sortable)

content.initial_state: 25 rows, each a national flag + country + a bar for sleep minutes, sorted by sleep descending (South Africa top, Austria bottom)
content.trigger: Toggle buttons: 'Sleep' / 'Paid work' re-sort and re-scale the bars
content.transition: Rows animate to their new order with a 300ms ease; bars re-length
content.payoff: Readers see the same 25 countries rearrange completely between sleep and work, making the 'who sleeps vs who works' contrast tactile

des_06.brief: A flag-labelled horizontal bar ranking that flips between sleep (ana_03) and paid work (ana_04) on toggle. Each row: flag_<country>.png + country name + value bar + h:mm label. Flags from the wikimedia cache (public domain). Caption notes the comparability caveat.
des_06.rationale: Real flags make the country dimension concrete and inviting; letting readers re-sort turns two static rankings into one exploration.

des_07.label: Housework gender gap by country (diverging bar with flags)

content.interaction: hover for women/men minutes and the gap in h:mm

style.palette: single warm ramp by gap size

des_07.brief: Horizontal bar of all 25 countries ranked by the unpaid-work gender gap (women minus men, minutes/day). Peru (290.8) at top, US (79.6) at bottom, both highlighted. Optional small flag icon at the end of each bar. Tooltip shows each sex's level.
des_07.rationale: A ranked bar shows the full spread of the gap across societies and anchors the two extremes the prose names.

des_08.label: Sonification — the housework gap from widest to narrowest

content.why_audio: Hearing the 25-country gap descend from a high, tense pitch (Peru) to a low, settled one (US) makes the spread of inequality audible as well as visible.
content.trigger: Click 'Play the gap' below the diverging-bar chart
content.ui_form: chart-synced sonification — each country's bar highlights in turn as a Web Audio tone plays, pitch mapped to gap size; a soft generated ambient bed (screen_rise.wav) is offered separately as the section's atmosphere

content.prompt: Seven gentle marimba/synth tones rising step by step, calm contemplative, no vocals, ~12s

data_mapping.engine: Web Audio oscillator, one tone per country in ranked order

content.fallback: If audio is muted or unsupported, the diverging-bar chart alone communicates the full ranking; the play button shows a tooltip.
content.novelty_note: Not a detached tone card: the playback is bound to the chart, walking the reader down the ranked bars while the pitch falls with the gap.

des_08.brief: A click-to-play Web Audio sonification that steps through the 25 country gaps (ana_05) from widest to narrowest, highlighting each bar as its tone sounds, pitch falling with the gap. The generated screen_rise.wav serves as an optional ambient bed.
des_08.rationale: This dataset's ranked 25-value sequence is exactly the small ordered series sonification handles well, and it deepens the chart rather than decorating it.

des_09.label: Screen time by decade (line) + then-vs-now bars

content.interaction: hover for exact minutes; the sonification (des_08 engine) can step through total_screen by decade

des_09.brief: Three-line chart across decades (1960s-2020s): TV/radio, computer/internet, and total screen. The computer line climbs from near-zero; total screen rises throughout. Caption carries the primary-activity undercount caveat.
des_09.rationale: A line chart is the natural form for a six-decade trend and shows broadcast and computer screens rising together rather than substituting.

des_10.label: Then vs now — what the day traded
des_10.brief: Diverging bar of minute changes from pre-1980 to 2010+: screens and active leisure up (right), paid work and housework down (left). Sleep deliberately excluded from emphasis per editor note (convention-affected); show it greyed if included.
des_10.rationale: A diverging bar reads as a ledger of trades — what the modern day gained and gave up — matching the section's argument.

des_11.label: Convergence — the closing unpaid-work gap

content.interaction: hover for women, men, and the gap each decade

des_11.brief: Two lines (women, men) of unpaid-work minutes by decade with the shrinking gap shaded between them. The visual point: the women's line barely descends while the men's line climbs to meet it — convergence driven by men.
des_11.rationale: Shading the gap between two lines makes the asymmetric mechanism (men rising, women roughly flat) immediately readable.

des_12.label: Total-work invariance stat callout

content.label: total work per day — barely changed across six decades

des_12.brief: Large stat callout stating total work (paid+unpaid) stayed near-flat from the 1970s to the 2020s, reinforcing that the gender story is about composition, not total effort.
des_12.rationale: The invariance is a single striking idea best delivered as a headline number rather than another chart in a chart streak.

des_13.label: Closing stat — the second shift

content.label: longer total working day for women, every day

des_13.brief: Final stat callout: women's total working day runs 32.5 minutes longer than men's. Closes the fairness-ledger theme on the lead finding.
des_13.rationale: Ending on the lead finding's most human number leaves the reader on tension, not summary.

page_rhythm.tone: dark editorial with warm-amber and cool-teal accents — dawn-to-dusk palette echoing the hero
page_rhythm.text_visual_pattern: visual-first teaser, then text-then-visual per section, breaking any chart streak with the flag ranking, sonification and stat callouts
page_rhythm.anti_sameness_notes: Avoids the generic chart-after-chart rhythm: a guess-first slider opens, a flag ranking that re-sorts is the centrepiece, audio is a chart-bound sonification (not a tone card), and stat callouts punctuate rather than repeat charts.
page_rhythm.typography_notes: Georgia serif body; system-ui labels; 64-72px stat callouts in amber; section titles in small-caps tracking; pull the 2.26x and +32.5 min as oversized figures.
